source.title: Generalisation dynamics of online learning in over-parameterised neural networks
source.authors: Sebastian Goldt; Madhu S. Advani; Andrew M. Saxe; Florent Krzakala; L. Zdeborová

record.tranche_reason: Analyzes how network size, training-set size, weight decay, and minibatch size affect generalization using a teacher-student regression setup and a generalization-error measure.
record.gate_note: The study tests generalization dynamics in a synthetic teacher-student regression task. Its results do not test the versions' specified natural-label, image-classification, optimizer-comparison, large-batch epoch-budget, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example conditions; they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study measures teacher-student regression error as width, noise, learning rate and data availability vary. It does not establish zero training error or locate an interpolation threshold, so width relative to teacher size does not test V2's widening beyond the width needed to fit. Its minibatch experiments measure asymptotic error with changing data requirements, rather than V5's fixed-epoch comparisons. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate, provided the worsening with width is qualified by noisy teacher outputs and fixed learning rate. The authors derive online-learning error scaling with width, learning rate and noise; ReLU scaling is supported numerically. Weight decay did not help in their simulations. Finite-data nonlinear networks can benefit from excess width. They conclude that generalization depends jointly on the algorithm, learning rate, architecture and dataset.
record.recipe_differences: Two-layer teacher-student regression with noisy teacher-generated outputs, online or minibatch SGD, and final mean-squared error against the noiseless teacher; not natural-label classification or random-label memorization.
record.method_sensitivity: The size effect depends on training-set size and activation. Minibatch size lowers asymptotic error up to about ∼ 100 samples, then gains become minimal. Weight decay did not improve final error in the tested setup.

fits_no_version.finding: With noisy teacher outputs and fixed learning rate, online asymptotic regression error grows with excess student width. Finite-data nonlinear networks can instead perform best with K > M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In teacher-student regression, the width-generalization relationship depends on noise, activation, learning rate and training-set size; excess teacher-relative width is distinct from interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay increased final generalization error in the reported simulations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay can worsen asymptotic generalization in the tested teacher-student regression setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing minibatch size reduced asymptotic error until gains became small around a batch size of order 100, while preserving the qualitative width dependence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger minibatches can improve asymptotic teacher-student regression error when additional data are available.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST images and matched Gaussian inputs produced similar error-versus-width curves with teacher-generated targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested MNIST input structure did not materially change width-dependent generalization in this regression setup.

record.problems: The main analytical result assumes the thermodynamic limit and a training set large enough that each sample is visited once. Finite-set results are simulations; the authors state that a complete analytical treatment remains open. Several comparisons are described qualitatively or shown in figures, with no exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately recoverable numeric values were reported in the prose for individual plotted points in Figs. 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, or 12. The selected rows record the text's stated qualitative results rather than estimating values from plots.

untested.parts: Almost-perfect random-label fitting alongside natural-label held-out accuracy and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test-error improvement after widening beyond an established zero-training-error threshold; the specified ReLU classification experiments.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and their dependence on tuning.
Large-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlations with generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples and measuring test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions, although the rows' qualitative regression findings are supported. No missing result directly tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization alongside natural-label generalization; the study uses noisy labels generated by a teacher network.
The specified ReLU experiments on natural MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10, and test error after fitting those datasets.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparisons on image-classification or language benchmarks.
Large-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets on image classifiers or language models.
Dropout comparisons, including its interaction with data augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Identifying and removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: sigmoidal student network
rows.size_stated: K hidden units; teacher M = 4 in Fig. 6
rows.operation_detail: Varied student size L = K − M and measured final generalization error after online SGD with a large training set.
rows.measure: Final generalization error ε*g versus L
rows.value: For large training sets (P = 50), the best generalisation is obtained by a network that matches the teacher size, K = M.
rows.note: Qualitative description of the plotted result; no exact values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The reported width trend is supported, but this row describes finite-data training, not online learning. Figure 6 uses 50N samples (N = 784), with samples revisited. K = M is a teacher-size comparison, not an established interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: linear student network
rows.size_stated: K hidden units; teacher M = 4 in Fig. 6
rows.operation_detail: Varied student size L = K − M and measured final generalization error after training on finite datasets.
rows.measure: Final generalization error ε*g versus L
rows.value: The bigger the network, the worse the performance for both P = 4 and P = 50; the optimal network has K = 1 hidden units.
rows.note: Qualitative description; the text does not give exact plotted values.
rows.check: The qualitative result is supported. Figure 6's P = 4 and P = 50 denote datasets containing 4N and 50N samples. Linear regression width comparisons do not measure V2's post-interpolation ReLU classification effect.

rows.subject: sigmoidal student network
rows.size_stated: K hidden units; teacher M = 4 in Fig. 6
rows.operation_detail: Varied student size L = K − M and measured final generalization error after training on a finite dataset.
rows.measure: Final generalization error ε*g versus L
rows.value: For P = 4, the best generalisation is obtained with networks that have K > M.
rows.note: Qualitative description; no exact plotted values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The qualitative result is supported, but the dataset contains 4N samples, not four samples. Better performance at K > M does not establish improvement beyond a zero-training-error threshold.

rows.subject: ReLU student network
rows.size_stated: K hidden units; teacher M = 4 in Fig. 6
rows.operation_detail: Varied student size L = K − M and measured final generalization error after training on a finite dataset.
rows.measure: Final generalization error ε*g versus L
rows.value: For P = 4, the best generalisation is obtained with networks that have K > M.
rows.note: Qualitative description; no exact plotted values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The qualitative result is supported, but the dataset contains 4N samples. The study does not establish zero training error or locate the fitting threshold; K > M denotes excess width relative to the teacher.

rows.subject: student networks
rows.operation_detail: Added weight decay by choosing κ > 0 and compared final generalization error with κ = 0.
rows.value: The authors report that they did not find a scenario where weight decay did not increase final generalisation error compared to κ = 0.
rows.note: The text states this as a finding across their simulations; Fig. 10 is described as illustrative.
rows.check: The reported worsening with weight decay is supported. It does not test dropout, adaptive optimizers or another listed version; 'reversed' has no applicable claim version here.

rows.subject: sigmoidal student network
rows.operation_detail: Varied minibatch size and student size; measured asymptotic generalization error.
rows.value: Increasing the mini-batch size lowers the asymptotic generalisation error up to a certain mini-batch size of order ∼ 100 samples, after which it stays roughly constant; minibatches do not change the scaling of ε*g with L.
rows.note: The main text gives a qualitative summary; no exact minibatch-specific error values are stated.
rows.check: The asymptotic minibatch result is supported. Appendix E states that larger batches require proportionally more data at a fixed number of updates; this is not a fixed-epoch-budget comparison.

rows.subject: ReLU student network
rows.operation_detail: Varied minibatch size and student size; measured asymptotic generalization error.
rows.value: Increasing the mini-batch size lowers the asymptotic generalisation error up to a certain mini-batch size of order ∼ 100 samples, after which it stays roughly constant; minibatches do not change the scaling of ε*g with L.
rows.note: The main text gives a qualitative summary; no exact minibatch-specific error values are stated.
rows.check: The asymptotic minibatch result is supported, but it does not measure the fixed-epoch generalization penalty in V5.

rows.subject: student networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared generalization error across Gaussian inputs and MNIST image inputs.

conditions.value: regression with outputs generated by a random teacher

rows.measure: Final generalization error ε*g versus L
rows.value: Switching to MNIST inputs reproduced the same ε*g-L curve as having Gaussian inputs to within the experimental error.
rows.uncertainty: within the experimental error; numerical uncertainty not stated
rows.note: MNIST labels were not used; this remained a teacher-generated regression task.
rows.check: The input-distribution comparison is supported. Appendix F describes finite MNIST and Gaussian datasets of matched size, so an unqualified online-learning description would be misleading. Targets remain teacher-generated regression outputs; no natural-label classification version is tested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
